1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.c4.strategy: The principled move: the c-pawn adds to the grip on d5 and takes space, and White decides later what kind of game it will be. Black has to choose a set-up at once: occupy the centre, fight for e4 with a bishop, or fianchetto on the queenside.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bf4.strategy: Puts the dark-squared bishop outside the pawn chain before a pawn on e3 can shut it in, and eyes the e5 square. The set-up is solid, easy to learn and light on theory, but it asks little of Black, who can develop freely and challenge d4 with a pawn.
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bf4.name: Indian Defence: London System
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bf4.background: The London System takes its name from the London tournament of 1922, where it appeared seven times, in games by Capablanca, Alekhine and Rubinstein. James Mason had been the first master-level player to use it regularly, including at the Vienna tournament of 1882.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain and pins the f6 knight to the queen, so Black cannot use that knight freely. White aims for quick, quiet development and a later kingside attack; the price is that the bishop no longer covers b2 and can be harassed.
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5.name: Torre Attack: Classical Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5.background: The Torre Attack is named after the Mexican grandmaster Carlos Torre Repetto, who beat the former world champion Emanuel Lasker with it. Tartakower, Spassky and, early in his career, Petrosian also played it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3.strategy: Supports the d4 pawn and opens the f1-bishop, the quiet way to build a sturdy centre. White keeps the plan open: a bishop on d3 and a well-timed e4 break, or the queen's bishop on the long diagonal. The cost is a c1-bishop hemmed in behind the pawns until the plan is chosen.
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3.name: Yusupov-Rubinstein System

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece and watches e4 and d5, but blocks the c-pawn, so White gives up the space-gaining c4 push. Black can pin the knight against the king with the bishop or take the centre at once, and White is left with a sound position and no clear plan.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5 c5.strategy: The most active answer: Black hits d4 before White's set-up gets going, and the bishop on g5 has not yet found a job. White must either support the centre quietly or sacrifice a pawn for activity. Black gets queenside space and a healthy game.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5 d5.strategy: Takes the centre at once and reaches a solid structure in which White's bishop is already committed to g5. The f6 knight stays pinned to the queen until the dark-squared bishop breaks the pin. Safe and simple, but the c8-bishop is shut in behind the e6 pawn for a long time.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5 h6.strategy: Puts the question to the bishop before Black has committed the centre: White must either keep the pin and risk a pawn attack on the bishop, or give it up for the knight. It costs a tempo and loosens the kingside a little, but it removes the bishop's sting early.
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5 h6.name: Torre Attack: Classical Defence, Nimzowitsch Variation

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 c5.strategy: Hits d4 at once, so White cannot build the centre in peace. Black gets queenside space and counterplay, and the central pawn structure is decided early: White must keep d4 supported or release the tension. The most direct way to meet the quiet set-up.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 b6.strategy: Prepares the queen's bishop on the long diagonal, so Black fights for e4 from a distance instead of occupying the centre with pawns. It is flexible and comfortable, but it leaves White free to build the centre, and Black has to be ready to meet a later e4 break.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Nc3 d5.strategy: Takes the centre at once. With White's knight already on c3 and no c-pawn push to attack d5, the pawn is only hit by a knight and stands securely. Black gets the classical solid structure, and White must find a plan without the usual space gain.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5 c5 4.e3.strategy: The solid reply: it defends d4 and opens the way for the f1-bishop, keeping the Torre set-up intact. White accepts that the bishop has left b2 without cover, so the b-pawn needs watching, and plays for a calm build-up and a kingside attack against Black's queenside space.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5 c5 4.e4.name: Torre Attack: Wagner Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5 c5 4.e4.strategy: A pawn sacrifice to blow the centre open while the bishop pins the f6 knight, with the e-pawn ready to push at the pinned piece. Black can simply take the pawn and has no pressing problem to solve, so White gives up material for a short-lived initiative.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5 c5 4.e3 b6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop, which will fight for the e4 square and the long diagonal from a distance. The pawn also keeps c5 well guarded. Black leaves the centre alone for now and bets on piece pressure against White's centre rather than on occupying space.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5 c5 4.e3 b6 5.d5.name: Torre Attack: Classical Defence, Petrosian Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5 c5 4.e3 b6 5.d5.strategy: A pawn sacrifice to cut across Black's set-up and keep the pin on f6. Black does best to take with the e-pawn, keeping the extra pawn and the knight safe. Taking with the knight is a blunder: the knight leaves f6 and Bxd8 wins the queen for a bishop.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 b6 4.Bd3.strategy: Develops the bishop on the diagonal that points at h7 and prepares castling. It also stands guard over e4, the square White wants for a central break, and meets Black's long-diagonal bishop on the same battleground. A natural, harmonious step in the system.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 b6 4.Bd3 Bb7.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop bears down on e4 and the f3 knight, and Black decides the centre later. The two bishops now face each other over e4, which makes White's central break harder to carry out and leaves a flexible game for both sides.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 c5 4.Bd3.strategy: Develops the bishop behind a well-supported d4 pawn and aims it at the kingside. White prepares castling and keeps the e4 break in the background, letting Black choose how to deal with the tension on d4. The standard route into the Colle structures.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 c5 4.Bd3 d5.strategy: Black builds the classical centre and takes the e4 square away from White's central break, which the bishop on d3 was preparing. The cost is a hemmed-in c8-bishop behind the e6 pawn, but the structure is solid and the game turns on how White supports d4.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 c5 4.Bd3 d5 5.c3.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 c5 4.Bd3 d5 5.c3.background: The Colle System was popularised in the 1920s by the Belgian master Edgard Colle and developed further by George Koltanowski; each won several tournaments with it in the 1920s and 1930s.
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 c5 4.Bd3 d5 5.c3.strategy: The traditional set-up: the pawn backs d4 solidly and prepares a knight on d2 and a central break on e4. White trades some activity for a safe centre, and the c1-bishop stays shut in behind the pawns. A sound, low-risk system with a simple plan.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 c5 4.Bd3 d5 5.b3.name: Rubinstein Opening
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 c5 4.Bd3 d5 5.b3.strategy: Opens the long diagonal for the queen's bishop instead of shutting it in behind a pawn on c3, aiming for a kingside attack behind a modest-looking set-up. The cost is a d4 pawn with no c3 pawn behind it, and the c-pawn stays free for a later strike.

Develops with pressure on d4: with the c5 pawn, Black attacks it twice, and White has to keep guarding it. Black stakes out the queenside and prepares quick castling, challenging White's quiet set-up to show a real plan.

Secures the king before the centre is settled, so the bishop on d3 can aim at the kingside in earnest. White is ready to bring the queen's bishop to the long diagonal, and the plan is a slow build-up for a kingside attack, not an immediate fight for the centre.

The most active square: the bishop looks at White's kingside along the diagonal to h2 and supports a later central advance, while Black's king gets ready to castle. Black has a harmonious, well-placed army against the attack.

The more modest square: the bishop stays behind the pawns and shields the king. It is solid and safe against a kingside attack, but it does less than a bishop on d6 and leaves Black passively placed if White gets the long diagonal working.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bg5.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Veresov Attack, Classical Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bg5.strategy: Pins the f6 knight to the queen, so Black's knight cannot move freely. Black has simple ways to break the pin, so White gets some pressure and a flexible game, not a lasting edge.
